name: Tunisia
summary: Independent from France in 1956; under Habib Bourguiba it gave women unusual legal rights; its 2010–11 revolution started the Arab Spring.

knownFor.label: Code of Personal Status
knownFor.note: Banned polygamy and gave women rights.

location.value: North Africa; area 163,610 km²; capital and largest city Tunis.

terrain.value: A Mediterranean coastline with the Sahel plain, the Dorsal mountains and Medjerda valley in the north, and salt lakes and the Sahara in the south.

climate.value: Mediterranean in the north with mild wet winters and hot summers, becoming semi-arid and desert in the south.

resources.value: Phosphates from the Gafsa basin, olive oil (among the world’s largest exporters), some oil and gas, and dates.

disasters.value: Droughts that hurt farming, floods such as those of 1969, and summer wildfires.

population.value: 11,972,169 at the 2024 census (infobox); the text says 12.1 million without giving a year.

urbanisation.value: About two-thirds of people live in cities; Tunis is the capital and largest city, followed by Sfax and Sousse.

disease.value: A good public health system by regional standards, with life expectancy in the mid-70s.

migration.value: Many Tunisians emigrated to work in France and Italy; others have crossed the Mediterranean by boat in recent years.

economicBase.value: Tourism was 7% of GDP and 370,000 jobs in 2009; the Sahel is among the world’s premier olive-growing areas; industry is mainly clothing and footwear, with car parts and electrical machinery. Phosphates are not covered in the part read.

tradeRoutes.value: Most trade is with the European Union under a 1995 association agreement, through ports such as Radès, Sfax and Bizerte.

moneyAndTax.value: The Tunisian dinar, introduced in 1958 to replace the franc; income taxes and value-added tax.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: The republic was declared on 25 July 1957 with Bourguiba as first president; after a 2022 referendum (about 30% turnout) approved a new constitution strengthening the presidency, Tunisia became a unitary presidential republic.

keyRulers.value: Habib Bourguiba (prime minister at independence on 20 March 1956, president 1957–87, declared unfit in November 1987); Zine El Abidine Ben Ali (ousted on 14 January 2011, after 23 or 24 years); Kais Saied (sworn in 23 October 2019, suspended parliament on 25 July 2021, re-elected on 6 October 2024 with over 90% on a 28.8% turnout).

succession.value: Bourguiba was removed in 1987 and Ben Ali fled in 2011; since then presidents have been chosen in popular elections.

institutions.value: Assembly of the Representatives of the People.

stability.value: Ben Ali took the presidency from Habib Bourguiba in November 1987 (7 November was celebrated as a holiday); he resigned and fled on 14 January 2011. On 25 July 2021 Kais Saied suspended parliament, dismissed the prime minister and withdrew MPs’ immunity.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A small, mostly non-political army, which stayed out of politics during the 2011 revolution.

majorWars.value: No major wars; French and Tunisian forces clashed at the Bizerte naval base in 1961.

territoryChange.value: French protectorate from 12 May 1881 (Treaty of Bardo); independence from France on 20 March 1956; republic declared on 25 July 1957.

alliancesRivals.value: Joined the Arab League in 1958 and the African Union; close ties with France, the EU and the United States.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Free schooling was expanded after 1956, and the University of Tunis was founded in 1960; literacy is high.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Railways, motorways, the Tunis light rail, and Tunis–Carthage airport.

religion.value: Around 98% Muslim in the text, 99% Sunni in the infobox. The Maliki school and the Jewish community are not covered in the part read.

languageWriting.value: Arabic is the official language and Tunisian Arabic is spoken daily; French is widely used in business and education.

artsArchitecture.value: The Medina of Tunis, the Great Mosque of Kairouan, Roman mosaics in the Bardo Museum, and malouf music.

socialStructure.value: A large urban middle class, with poorer rural and inland regions and high youth unemployment.

sharedIdentity.value: A Tunisian identity mixing Arab, Berber, Islamic and Mediterranean heritage.

dailyLife.value: Couscous, brik pastries and harissa chilli paste; café culture in towns.

neighbours.value: Algeria to the west, Libya to the south-east, and Italy across the Mediterranean.

ideasReligions.value: The 1956 Code of Personal Status banned polygamy and gave women more rights; the 2011 revolution began the Arab Spring.

colonisation.value: A French protectorate from the Treaty of Bardo in 1881 until independence in 1956.

riseSignals.value: Legend credits Dido of Tyre with founding Carthage in 814 BC, as told by Timaeus of Tauromenium.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; it was seen as a democratic model after the 2011 revolution.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still in existence as an independent republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
